text_en: These days it has become normal to write on a computer or smartphone. Even if you can't recall a kanji, the machine converts it instantly. The convenience goes without saying, but haven't we lost something as chances to write by hand have declined? According to one study, content is easier to remember when written by hand. That is probably because, as we move our hands, we sort out in our heads what we should write. That said, I have no intention of rejecting machines. What matters is using each according to the purpose. One approach is to use pen and paper while developing your ideas, and a computer for the final copy. What is called for is an attitude of mastering our tools rather than being used by them.

On one prefecture's local line, ridership has fallen to a third of its peak, and losses have continued. The railway company proposed switching to buses, but residents pushed back hard. For elderly people and high-school students who don't drive, the railway is an essential means of getting around. So the local authority came up with a plan to turn the station into a hub for community interaction. When a reading corner and a café were set up in the station building, even people who weren't taking the train began gathering there. Although ridership still can't be called sufficient, the decline is starting to be checked. This can be seen as an attempt to rethink the railway not merely as transport but as an asset of the town.

What matters is neither dismissing new words out of hand nor using them uncritically. It is acquiring the ability to choose appropriate words for the person and the situation.
